title: Bragg Mirror
experiment: Bragg reflection from a crystal (Davisson–Germer, distributed Bragg reflector)
intro: To the right is a crystal: a row of low ridges, period 1.8, each 2 high. At most speeds the packet has more energy than any ridge and sails through. Yet at one speed the crystal is a near-perfect mirror. Tune the speed so the packet comes back to the target on the left.
goal: Choose the speed |k₀| at which the crystal reflects the packet back onto the target behind it. You may observe from t = 8.

physics.point: Each ridge reflects a little. When the round trip between neighbouring ridges is a whole wavelength, all those small echoes add in phase: the Bragg condition 2a = λ inside the crystal.

idea: In 1927 Davisson and Germer fired electrons at a nickel crystal and found them reflected strongly only at particular energies and angles, exactly where X-rays obey Bragg's law for the same crystal. It was the first proof that electrons are waves.

A single low ridge reflects almost nothing when the particle has more energy than the ridge is high. A row of them reflects a little at each one. Usually the echoes have random phases and cancel. When twice the spacing is a whole number of wavelengths, every echo returns in step with the others and they add up: the crystal becomes a mirror.

In band language, that wavelength sits at the edge of the Brillouin zone, where the periodic potential opens a gap: there is no travelling wave inside the crystal at that energy, only a decaying one, so the wave has to go back.
maths: The ridges are V sin²(πx/a) = V/2 − (V/2) cos(2πx/a), with a = 1.8 and V = 2. The constant part V/2 raises the floor, so inside the crystal k_in² = k₀² − 2·V/2 = k₀² − V. The cosine couples k_in to k_in − 2π/a; the two match (a standing wave) when

The gap in energy is V/2 = 1 (its Fourier component V/4, doubled), wide enough that the 8 periods here reflect a sizeable band of speeds around it. The soft edges of the crystal and the packet's speed spread (Δk = 1/(2σ) ≈ 0.17) move the measured optimum slightly down, to about k₀ ≈ 2.15:
The energy E = k₀²/2 ≈ 2.3 at the optimum is above the ridge height 2: a classical particle would cross every ridge.
try: Launch at k₀ = 2.8: the packet passes the crystal almost untouched.
Scan k₀ from 2.8 down to 1.9 and watch the reflected packet grow, peak and shrink again.
At the slowest speed allowed, k₀ = 1.6, the energy 1.28 is below the ridges, yet most of it gets through the thin ridges and only about 16% comes back.
